section_title: What do the believers pray for after the threats?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 23 On their release, Peter and John returned to their own people and reported everything that the chief priests and elders had said to them. 24 When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord. “Sovereign Lord,” they said, “You made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. 25 You spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Your servant, our father David: ‘Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? 26 The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against His Anointed One.’ 27 In fact, this is the very city where Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed. 28 They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.

29 And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness, 30 as You stretch out Your hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of Your holy servant Jesus.” 31 After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.

context_lines: After their release, Peter and John report the threats to the other believers. The community turns to God together, addressing Him as the sovereign Creator. Their prayer begins with who God is and what He has spoken.

They quote Psalm 2 and connect its opposition to the Lord’s Anointed with the actions of Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and people of Israel against Jesus. Those actions were real opposition, yet God’s purpose was not defeated.

The prayer then names the present threats and asks for boldness to speak God’s word, alongside healing and signs through Jesus’s name. The meeting place is shaken, the believers are filled with the Spirit, and they speak boldly. Luke connects their request with the answer he records.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as a prayer for God’s work to continue through threatened witnesses, with the Spirit giving fresh boldness. [Wesley on verse 31](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-acts-of-the-apostles/) describes them as filled afresh, and [Calvin on verse 31](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/acts/4.htm) emphasizes both the sign of God’s presence and the practical answer of strengthened witness.
god_plan_lines: The believers explicitly apply [Psalm 2:1–2](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/2.htm) to the opposition against Jesus. The wider psalm places the nations’ hostility alongside God’s established King and His purpose for the nations. Their prayer rests on that larger view of whose purposes will stand.

[Ephesians 6:18–20](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/6.htm) gives a later echo: Paul asks believers to pray that he will proclaim the gospel fearlessly while in chains. Prayer supports the witness of God’s people through hardship as the mission continues.
current_position_lines: Prayer and Faith reads this as a specific request aimed at God’s purpose: boldness to proclaim His word and His power at work through Jesus’s name. What Does Prayer Look Like? also emphasizes the believers’ desire to remain faithful under pressure. The account records God strengthening them for the witness they have asked to continue.
